criteria.descriptor: All technical claims are correct: TP shards matmuls and requires a per-layer all-reduce that is bandwidth-bound (belongs on NVLink intra-node); PP passes only boundary activations, tolerates InfiniBand, but has decode bubbles; data parallelism needs a full copy and cannot host an oversized model; KV cache scales with batch × context × layers; continuous batching and PagedAttention are correctly described; K8s facts (nvidia.com/gpu per-node granularity, gang scheduling, cold-start components) are accurate. Deduct for inverting the TP/PP interconnect argument, calling data parallelism a fit, or fabricated numbers/primitives.

Addresses all four parts (a sharding + why not DP; b TP-vs-PP over this topology; c throughput without breaking TTFT; d autoscaling/cold start). Full marks require the KV-cache consideration and the autoscaling cold-start reality; partial credit if one part (commonly c or d) is thin or missing.

Every recommendation is tied to its mechanism — TP intra-node because the all-reduce is on the critical path and NVLink >> InfiniBand; PP only across nodes because it trades bandwidth for bubbles; scale on queue depth because reactive GPU-util HPA lags minutes-long cold starts. Reward explicit trade-off reasoning over a bare list of correct choices.

Design-review-quality exposition: organized by the four parts, uses precise vocabulary (tensor/pipeline parallelism, all-reduce, KV cache, continuous batching, gang scheduling, HPA/KEDA) correctly, and is concise enough for a reviewer to follow the argument without re-reading.

expected_answer_points: Recognizes 140 GB of weights exceeds one 80 GB GPU so the model must be sharded, and explains that data parallelism cannot help because it requires a full model copy per replica.
Chooses tensor parallelism within a single node so the per-layer all-reduce collective runs over high-bandwidth NVLink.

Contrasts TP (frequent all-reduce on the critical path, bandwidth-sensitive, keep intra-node) with PP (only activation passing at stage boundaries, tolerates InfiniBand but suffers pipeline bubbles / poor decode utilization), and concludes TP-only fits in one node here.
Accounts for KV-cache growth with concurrency and context length, sizing shard degree for headroom and using PagedAttention to manage/avoid KV fragmentation.

Uses continuous / in-flight batching for high utilization and names the latency-vs-throughput trade-off (large prefill stalling decode / hurting p95 TTFT), with mitigation like chunked prefill or prioritizing decode.

Identifies cold-start reality — node provisioning + multi-GB image pull + loading 140 GB of weights takes minutes — so reactive HPA on GPU utilization lags spikes; scales on queue depth/concurrency (KEDA) with a warm/over-provisioned buffer and pre-pulled images.
Notes scaling granularity is a whole TP replica (one 8-GPU node via nvidia.com/gpu) and that multi-node replicas need gang/coscheduling (Volcano/Kueue) to avoid partial-start deadlock.
common_pitfalls: Proposing data parallelism / replicating the model to 'scale', not recognizing that each replica still needs a full 140 GB copy that won't fit on one 80 GB GPU.
Recommending tensor parallelism spread across nodes over InfiniBand, ignoring that the per-layer all-reduce is on the critical path and the ~10× slower cross-node link will break the TTFT SLO.
Treating pipeline parallelism as free for inference, overlooking pipeline bubbles and poor GPU utilization during single-token autoregressive decode.
Sizing GPU memory for weights only and ignoring the KV cache, which dominates memory at high concurrency and long context and is the real capacity limiter.
Assuming standard HPA on GPU utilization handles the 50→800 spike, ignoring minutes-long cold starts from node provisioning, multi-GB image pulls, and loading 140 GB of weights.
Forgetting that a replica consumes a whole 8-GPU node and that multi-node replicas need gang/coscheduling, so partially scheduled pods deadlock waiting for GPUs.
reference_answer:
(a) Sharding. FP16 weights are ~140 GB (70B × 2 bytes), which exceeds a single 80 GB A100, so this is a model-parallel problem, not a data-parallel one — data parallelism needs a full copy of the model per replica, so it cannot host a model that won't fit on one GPU (it only scales throughput of a model that already fits). I'd use tensor parallelism (TP) across the 8 GPUs inside one node. TP shards each layer's weight matrices row/column-wise so every GPU computes part of each matmul; at TP=8 the per-GPU weight footprint drops to ~17.5 GB, leaving most of each 80 GB card for KV cache and activations.

(b) TP vs PP given the interconnect. TP inserts an all-reduce on the critical path of every forward pass (two per transformer layer, Megatron-style: after attention and after the MLP), so it is extremely sensitive to interconnect bandwidth. NVLink inside the node (hundreds of GB/s) makes that collective cheap; InfiniBand between nodes is roughly an order of magnitude slower, so running TP across nodes would drop a slow collective into the token-generation loop and blow the TTFT SLO. Pipeline parallelism (PP) instead splits the model into stage-groups of layers and only passes activations point-to-point at stage boundaries — far less traffic, tolerant of InfiniBand — but it introduces pipeline bubbles: autoregressive decode emits one token at a time, so stages sit idle unless many in-flight requests keep the pipeline full. Rule of thumb: keep TP intra-node over NVLink, and only reach for PP to span nodes when a model won't fit in one node. Here 70B fits in one 8×80 GB node, so TP-only (TP=4 or 8) is correct and avoids cross-node collectives entirely.

(c) Throughput at 50–800 concurrency. Use a server with continuous / in-flight batching (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM) that schedules at the iteration level so new requests join the running batch instead of waiting for it to drain, plus PagedAttention to page KV-cache blocks and avoid fragmentation. Size the TP degree so the KV cache — which grows with batch × context length × layers — has headroom at peak concurrency. Manage the latency/throughput trade-off: bigger batches raise throughput, but a large prefill can stall decodes and hurt p95 TTFT, so use chunked prefill and prioritize decode tokens.

(d) Autoscaling on Kubernetes. A replica = the whole TP group = one 8-GPU node (requested via nvidia.com/gpu), so scaling granularity is a full node; any multi-node (PP) replica needs gang/coscheduling (Volcano/Kueue) so all its pods start together or none do, avoiding partial-allocation deadlock. Cold start is the hard part: provisioning a GPU node (Karpenter/cluster-autoscaler, minutes) + pulling a multi-GB CUDA image + loading 140 GB of weights can take minutes, so reactive HPA on GPU utilization lags the spike badly. Mitigate by scaling on queue depth/concurrency (KEDA) rather than lagging utilization, keeping a warm over-provisioned buffer (baseline replicas plus low-priority placeholder pods for headroom), pre-pulling images to nodes, and speeding weight load with local NVMe or weight streaming.
